top.line: A 2024 Lisbon talk on GenAI mostly still holds
top.para: On 28 June 2024 at OWASP Global AppSec EU in Lisbon, the talk Deterministic GenAI Outputs with Provenance ran 132 slides and demoed The Cyber Boardroom. It called Portuguese a programming language, set out principles such as graphs instead of RAG, and challenged Portugal. Two years on, provenance and graphs hold and models became agents.

in-short.line: Portuguese is a programming language, and graphs beat RAG
in-short.para: The talk at OWASP Global AppSec EU in June 2024 used 132 slides and a live demo. Portuguese ranked sixth by speakers as a programming language. GenAI matters because it understands. Principles included read-only models and graphs over RAG, with a challenge for Portugal to lead. Two years later, models have become agents.

talk.line: Deterministic outputs with provenance was the whole argument
talk.para: On Friday 28 June 2024, in the last session before OWASP Global AppSec EU closed at the Lisbon Congress Centre, the talk Deterministic GenAI Outputs with Provenance was given. Its slides, video and transcript are online. The title carried the argument: traceability, source tracking, lineage and origin verification for GenAI output.

language.line: Prompts made Portuguese the sixth most powerful programming language
language.para: Because prompts are written in natural language, Portuguese, with 236 million first-language speakers, counts as a programming language. The talk asked for models for Portuguese from Portugal, Angola, Mozambique and Cape Verde. In 2026 Portugal released Amália, an open European Portuguese model built on EuroLLM; the other varieties still wait.

understanding.line: GenAI matters for understanding content, and graphs beat RAG
understanding.para: GenAI's value is understanding, not creating; hallucinations help creativity but harm facts. Principles were read-only models, bringing your own content, assuming prompts are exposed and using graphs instead of RAG. These became the newsroom's provenance rule and fractal semantic graphs, while the threat moved from a model answering to an agent with tools.

boardroom.line: The Cyber Boardroom briefed boards in their own language
boardroom.para: The live demo showed The Cyber Boardroom, built open source over two months, answering a board member in several languages, with three personas, a fourth model reviewing them and Athena, the security advisor. Personalised briefings for risk owners remain central, but one assistant has become teams of agents with roles, mandates and records.

challenge.line: Portugal must lead, or become another technology consumer
challenge.para: The talk ended telling the Portuguese audience that the country's future depends on them, otherwise Portugal becomes just another consumer of global technology. The challenge echoes 2010 and 2016, with the lever moving from security to code to language. Amália suggests some of it was heard.

limits.line: A first documented demo, not the cause of Amália
limits.para: It was not the first mention of The Cyber Boardroom, only its first documentable live demo in Portugal. The talk is not claimed to have led to Amália, since many people asked for a Portuguese model. The commentary is from now; the slides and transcript are from 2024.

sources.line: Sources: the talk page, transcript and Amália reports
sources.para: The piece comes from a voice memo of 16 October 2026. Every quote is taken from the talk's page on diniscruz.ai, with its slides, video and transcript. Current details on Amália come from The Next Web and the model's technical report, read on 16 October 2026.
